newsitem.title: BELGIUM: West made no pledge to Moscow, NATO told.
newsitem.headline: West made no pledge to Moscow, NATO told.

text.p: Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze told NATO this week that the West did not offer Moscow any guarantees about the alliance's future during talks over German unification in 1990, NATO sources said on Thursday.

The sources said Shevardnadze's comments, made to NATO Secretary General Javier Solana during a meeting in Tbilisi on Wednesday, contradict Russian claims that NATO's enlargement plans represent broken promises by the West.

Shevardnadze, who was Soviet foreign minister when Moscow cut the deal in 1990 with Western powers opening the way for unification, told Solana that the talks only concerned Germany, the sources said.
Solana was in Tbilisi as part of a tour of former Soviet republics. Moscow has sharply criticised the tour as an attempt by NATO to come between Russia and its neighbours.
"President Shevardnadze told the secretary general that during those two-plus-four talks, no guarantees had been given concerning NATO enlargement," one source said.

"He wanted to set the record straight because Shevardnadze is aware that in recent months the Russian government has claimed that NATO enlargement contravenes a verbal assurance that NATO would not enlarge," the source said.
The two-plus-four talks involved East and West Germany, France, Britain, the United States and the Soviet Union.
Russia and NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, are at loggerheads over the alliance's plans to enlarge its membership into former Warsaw Pact countries.
Poland, Hungary, the Czech republic and possibly Slovenia are expected to be offered membership at a summit of NATO leaders in Spain this summer.
Former Soviet republics such as Georgia have partnership agreements with NATO but are not in line for membership.
Moscow views NATO enlargement as a threat that will play into the hands of nationalists and other anti-Western forces in Russia.
NATO diplomats say a general belief in Moscow that it was duped by the West during the two-plus-four talks may now be leading Russia to demand a water-tight treaty with NATO.
"It is a trauma for them which is making them ask for a legally binding treaty," one diplomat said.
NATO sources also said they believed Shevardnazde's comments about the two-plus-four talks may have triggered Moscow's outburst on Wednesday about Solana's trip. Sergei

Yastrzhembsky, President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary, told Interfax news agency that Solana's trip had "an undeclared, behind-the-scenes" aim -- to prevent any form of integration between the former Soviet republics.
